title: Triptych Migration Clinic: Mapping OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood
summary: Clinic-style migration demo focussing on concrete parity mappings for prompts and runtime behavior across OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood API. Covered integration patterns, differences in streaming and function calling, KV cache and batching recommendations, security posture, and an agreed pilot plan with benchmarking and SOC2 docs to follow.
next_steps: Maya to send parity mapping sheet and initial cost estimate (link) by 2026-10-15
Schedule 72-hour benchmark window with Crescent test traffic (Marcus + Tom) - target week of 2026-10-20
Share SOC2 plus KMS/HSM integration doc with Elena by 2026-10-16
Provision trial Redwood Dedicated tenant for Crescent (limited) - owner: Liam
action_items: Maya Chen - send parity spreadsheet + pricing - due 2026-10-15
Liam O'Connor - provision trial Dedicated tenant + guide for KV cache test - due 2026-10-18
Marcus Li (Crescent) - share representative request traces and percentiles - due 2026-10-14
Elena Park - confirm encryption/KMS questions and schedule 30-min follow-up - due 2026-10-16
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-13 16:00 UTC | Duration: 58 min | Attendees: Maya, Liam, Nadia, Tom (Redwood); Priya, Sam, Elena, Marcus (Crescent)

Summary: short clinic + hands-on parity mapping. Recording started.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to run a practical clinic today, sort of triage three upstream providers, openai, anthropic and together, map the client side changes and show the Redwood API parity paths. i think we have 50 minutes, should be enough to do a few prompts and then discuss security and next steps.

[00:18] Dr. Priya Nair: yup thanks maya, quick context—our stack is currently split. customer-facing assistant runs on OpenAI chat endpoints, batch rerank with Together models, and a couple of research experiments on Claude like anthropic. main asks: keep SLOs for latency, reduce token cost, and ensure PHI never leaves our VPC for certain endpoints.

[00:42] Sam Torres: also timeline is fairly tight, execs want a pilot within three weeks if numbers look good.

[00:50] Liam O'Connor: quick qualification, priya—can you share rough qps and typical sequence lengths so we can tune the demo?

[00:56] Marcus Li: sure baseline p99 is about 420ms on our openai calls for the chat assistant at 512 token max; overall 20 rps peak but bursts to 60 during morning hours, average seq len is 450 tokens, rerank jobs are offline but they want to move some rerank to nearline.

[01:20] Nadia Alvarez: and security—Elena flagged SOC2 plus internal KMS, correct?

[01:24] Elena Park: yes we need audit logs and key control, also SSO/SAML and RBAC. some data is considered PHI so ideally private deployment or VPC endpoints for those routes.

[01:40] Tom Hsu: great, we'll demo three things: code parity for chat/generate, streaming and function/tool-calling differences, and then runtime tuning notes: batching, kv cache and quantization suggestions.

[02:05] Maya Chen: ok starting the parity mapping doc share—(link pasted) this sheet has four columns: upstream call pattern, customer code snippet, Redwood API equivalent, and notes on behavioral diffs. first example is openai chat-completions with messages array.

[02:24] [Screen share noise; brief pause]

[02:30] Liam O'Connor: with openai you'd send messages role:user,... for function calling there are function schemas, anthropic has a different assistant prompt ordering, together has slightly different tokenization quirks. on Redwood the mapping is pretty straightforward: you call the /v1/generate or /v1/chat endpoints, same messages structure, but we expose explicit model variants for compatibility. important note: streaming chunk boundary semantics may differ slightly—some clients expect the delta to always contain a complete token, we stream byte deltas. so if you rely on exact chunking you may see a shift.

[03:05] Sam Torres: ok so we need to test streaming because the client UI replays partial tokens for typing. if chunk boundaries shift we could see jitter.

[03:12] Tom Hsu: yes recommend switching to idempotent framing on the client so minor chunk differences don't affect UX. we can point to a small client helper lib.

[03:26] [00:03:30 marker on call recorder]

[03:32] Dr. Priya Nair: on llm output diffs—how much retuning of system prompts do you anticipate? our prompts are sensitive, we have QA for hallucination thresholds.

[03:40] Liam O'Connor: depends on model family; for like-for-like variants we usually see micro-deltas, a handful of guardrail adjustments at most. for switching from openai gpt to our curated open model v3-compatible variant you'll see slight temperature behavior differences—we've captured those in the parity sheet with suggested prompt knobs.

[03:58] Maya Chen: i'll highlight the example where we mapped an openai function-call flow to Redwood's function calling. the main differences: Redwood includes structured schema validation on the server side, and there is an explicit finalize event in streaming when function return completes. customers sometimes miss that finalize and assume the last chunk equals completion.

[04:20] Elena Park: that finalize event—does it create extra audit events we can tie to our SIEM?

[04:26] Tom Hsu: yes all request/response lifecycle events are logged and can be exported; we support syslog/forwarders to SIEM and have both request-level and token-level metadata for debugging.

[04:40] [05:00 on recorder]

[04:44] Marcus Li: about private deployment—if we run Redwood Private on prem, how much of the control plane is in our network vs hosted? we can't have secret telemetry leaving the air-gapped clusters.

[04:55] Liam O'Connor: for Private we offer an optional disconnected mode. control plane can be customer-hosted; minimal outbound telemetry is configurable. we support HSM integrations for KMS and you can run the inference plane fully on-prem. there are tradeoffs: fewer autoscaling bells and whistles unless you wire up the orchestration hooks.

[05:20] Dr. Priya Nair: cost question: our CFO cares about both token cost and infra; what are ballpark savings moving from hosted openai to Redwood Dedicated?

[05:29] Nadia Alvarez: ballpark depends heavily on model choices and tokenization. for same-quality open model variants we typically see 20-45% cost reductions at scale due to batching, prefix cache and quantized kernel paths with Dedicated. we'll put model-specific estimates in the sheet.

[05:50] Sam Torres: performance parity—our p99 target is <=500ms for chat. can you meet that with Dedicated?

[05:57] Liam O'Connor: yes Dedicated with optimized kernels and continuous batching can hit sub-300ms p95 on the model profiles similar to your seq lengths, p99 depends on burst design; we recommend a hybrid routing policy: hosted for low-latency critical routes and Dedicated for bulk.

[06:20] [06:30 marker]

[06:28] Maya Chen: demo time—first quick code swap. original openai snippet: fetch openai.com/v1/chat/completions with messages. show switching to redwood client with the same messages and a model alias redwood/gpt-v3-compat.

[06:48] [Screen typing sounds]

[07:00] Tom Hsu: note the header differences: API key header name is X-Redwood-Key instead of Authorization Bearer by default, but our SDKs handle that. we showed a tiny adapter function to keep your existing auth plumbing.

[07:18] Marcus Li: small question—we use request ids propagated across services, will those survive?

[07:23] Liam O'Connor: yes you can pass x-request-id and we retain it in logs and traces. we also offer trace linking with OpenTelemetry.

[07:36] [07:45 on recorder]

[07:40] Maya Chen: next example is Together reranker migration. currently Sam's pipeline posts a batch of candidates to together rerank endpoint. we recommend two patterns: 1) nearline batch rerank on Redwood Dedicated GPU pool with larger batch sizes and low-cost quantized variant, or 2) hybrid where you use Redwood Hosted for synchronous small batches.

[08:05] Sam Torres: our rerank latency SLAs are loose, but throughput matters. nearline option sounds promising. any quota changes we should expect?

[08:12] Nadia Alvarez: Dedicated lets you run larger batches without per-request throttling; we can tune batch windows to limit tail latency. we also provide SLO configs so if you need max latency for interactive routes we won't batch aggressively there.

[08:30] [08:45 marker]

[08:46] Dr. Priya Nair: switching gears—KV cache behavior, we use long context synth for some multi-step dialogs. how is the Redwood KV cache compatible?

[08:55] Tom Hsu: Redwood exposes explicit KV cache controls; you can pin prefixes, snapshot and rehydrate, and we do prefix caching to reduce compute for repeated prefixes. noted caveat: TTL semantics differ from anthropic's early cache behavior—consult the sheet for migration notes.

[09:20] Elena Park: auditability of the cached items—are they stored encrypted at rest and do we get access logs for reads?

[09:27] Liam O'Connor: yes encrypted at rest with customer-managed KMS in Private mode; read/write access logs are emitted and can be forwarded to your SIEM. for Hosted we use multi-tenant encryption with tenant keys in KMS but Private gives you full control.

[09:45] [10:00 on recorder]

[09:50] Maya Chen: now quick live prompt comparison. i will run same assistant prompt through openai and our redwood/gpt-v3-compat variant and show diffs.

[10:04] [Audio click; test requests sent]

[10:10] Liam O'Connor: openai response—(reads partial): "Sure, here's a summary of the patient's symptoms..."

[10:18] Liam O'Connor: redwood response—(reads partial): "Here's a brief summary: 1) cough 2) elevated temp, potential dehydration". you can see minor phrasing differences, same facts.

[10:30] Dr. Priya Nair: any examples where hallucination changed materially? we can't tolerate patient attribute fabrications.

[10:36] Tom Hsu: we recommend safety classifiers and a defensive prompt layer; for critical PHI routes consider deterministic models or additional verification step. we'll surface risk estimations per prompt in the parity sheet.

[10:50] [11:00 marker]

[11:00] Sam Torres: about function calling—our code relies on functionSignature.ordering and sometimes downstream services expect exact key names. will Redwood enforce schema mismatches?

[11:09] Maya Chen: Redwood's function calling enforces schema if provided; we also return a structured error payload that is consistent which helps deterministic retries. note: if you omit schema it will fall back to best-effort. mapping rules in the sheet include common transformation snippets.

[11:30] Elena Park: ok security checklist—SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC yes?

[11:36] Nadia Alvarez: yes SAML SSO and SCIM are supported, RBAC is role-based with custom roles in Console. audit logs streams, retention configurable for Dedicated/Private. for Hosted we have default retention windows with upgrades available.

[11:50] Marcus Li: curious about encryption—do you support Customer-Managed Keys for Hosted?

[11:55] Liam O'Connor: currently Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer keys in supported clouds; for full HSM-backed key isolation Private is required. we'll include that matrix in the docs.

[12:10] [12:30 marker]

[12:15] Maya Chen: let's go through the proposed pilot plan. objective: 2-week pilot, measure latency, cost, and quality delta on a subset of traffic (15% of user requests). steps: provide sample traces, we'll provision a trial Dedicated tenant and a staging proxy, run A/B for 72 hours, then review metrics.

[12:40] Dr. Priya Nair: A/Bing is fine, we need blackout plan to switch back to OpenAI instantly if errors spike.

[12:46] Tom Hsu: built-in fallback routing is supported—we can route by policy and have automatic rollback on error thresholds.

[13:00] Sam Torres: who owns the benchmark run configurations?

[13:03] Liam O'Connor: Liam and Marcus will coordinate, we'll push a small harness, but Marcus must provide representative traces and schematics.

[13:20] [13:30 marker]

[13:25] Dr. Priya Nair: any legal/procurement notes? we have a standard data processing addendum and some regulatory clauses.

[13:31] Maya Chen: we have template DPAs and can add custom addenda for PHI-related clauses; for Private deployments that's easier to accommodate. I'll loop in our legal team after this call.

[13:45] Elena Park: can you provide SOC2 and penetration test reports?

[13:48] Nadia Alvarez: yes we'll share SOC2 and recent pentest summary. full reports under NDA; we'll send links.

[14:02] [14:30 marker]

[14:10] Marcus Li: license/price model question—how do per-token and infra fees combine?

[14:16] Maya Chen: Hosted is usage per-token; Dedicated mixes a committed infra fee plus usage discounts. pricing examples in the attached estimate. we can model a blended TCO for your expected volumes.

[14:35] Sam Torres: can you include together's rerank price baseline so we can compare?

[14:40] Nadia Alvarez: yes will include comparative baselines for all three upstreams.

[14:52] [15:00 marker]

[14:55] Maya Chen: quick console tour—showing per-route cost view, model selection, rollout policy, and canary settings. note the evals tab where you can pin prompt sets and track quality drift.

[15:18] [Screen share: Console UI]

[15:30] Dr. Priya Nair: nice, that evals tab looks useful for our QA team. can we upload our internal eval suites?

[15:36] Tom Hsu: yes you can upload CSVs or link to S3; we can run periodic evals and alert on regressions above thresholds.

[15:50] Elena Park: retention for eval artifacts? we need six months for audits.

[15:54] Nadia Alvarez: retention configurable on Dedicated/Private; Hosted by default is 90 days but enterprise add-on can extend to 12 months.

[16:10] [16:30 marker]

[16:05] Maya Chen: wrapping up—recap of next steps: we'll send parity mapping sheet and cost estimate, Crescent to send traces, Liam will spin up trial Dedicated tenant, Elena will review security docs. schedule benchmark window next week.

[16:24] Dr. Priya Nair: sounds good, thanks all.

[16:28] Sam Torres: appreciate the practical clinic, especially the streaming and function calling notes.

[16:33] Marcus Li: i'll add the traces to the shared folder by Friday.

[16:36] Elena Park: i'll review SOC2 and confirm KMS requirements.

[16:40] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, i'll follow up with links and timeline.

[16:45] [Recording stopped]

Post-call notes: parity sheet includes ~22 mappings across common patterns, streaming chunking differences annotated, function-calling validation examples, KV cache TTL notes, and a pilot checklist.

End of transcript.
